discursive

/dis-KUR-siv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Discursive means rambling from topic to topic; lacking a clear, direct structure.

The lecture was so discursive that students' notes wandered from beekeeping to tax law before ever touching the syllabus.

Example

The best man's toast began with how the couple met. Four minutes in, it had detoured through his own college roommate troubles, a theory about parallel parking, and a story involving a borrowed kayak that never reached its point. Guests kept lifting their glasses hopefully, only to lower them again. The toast was warm, even funny in places — but so discursive that when he finally said 'to the happy couple,' half the room had forgotten whose wedding it was.

The toast's detours through roommates, parking theories, and kayaks — with no through-line back to the couple — show the topic-to-topic rambling that discursive names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rambling: Rambling talk drifts on and on without direction, but each stretch of it still makes sense as you follow along. Discursive is its more formal cousin: writing or speech that wanders from topic to topic, losing the thread of its subject without ever losing plain sense.

meandering: Meandering means winding indirectly from point to point, the way a river takes the long way — slow, but connected the whole way. A discursive answer strays further: it leaves the route altogether, hopping between topics with no clear structure to bring it back.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

focused: held to a single clear point

concise: brief and tightly organized

Where it sits · how far the writing wanders off course — loose → discursive → incoherent

loose vs. discursive: Loose is weaker than discursive: loosely organized writing still follows its subject, just casually, while discursive writing wanders away from the subject altogether.

incoherent vs. discursive: Incoherent is stronger than discursive — incoherent writing has no traceable thread at all, while a discursive piece rambles yet can still be followed, detour by detour.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: apart; in different directions

Root — curs

Root — curs: to run (Latin currere, cursus)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Discursive decomposes perfectly: dis- ('apart, in different directions') + curs ('to run' — the root of cursor and courier) + -ive ('tending to'). Latin discurrere meant 'to run about in different directions,' so discursive speech is literally speech 'characterized by running off every which way.' The picture is built right into the morphemes: a discursive talker's thoughts are runners scattering from the starting line in different directions.

Use the root in a new word: courier

Use the root in a new word: courier: The signed contract left the office at noon and reached Tokyo by courier before the markets opened.
